b1: Two strangers agree to do a job. One is afraid to pay and get nothing. The other is afraid to deliver and never get paid. Neither wants to open another account just to do one transaction.
b2: This is Pact. It opens straight into a working guest workspace — no sign-up, no form, no email. Everything here is real: a live model, a durable database, and the actual PayPal Sandbox, not a mock. And the workspace is mine alone: another guest cannot see it.
b3: I post a job with a brief, acceptance criteria, and a budget ceiling of two hundred dollars. Seller agents quote, the buyer counters, and the price converges. Every round is recorded, and the budget is enforced in code — an agreement above the ceiling is rejected by the engine, not left to the model. Sellers are ranked by verified-delivery reputation, so an unreliable seller has to be cheaper to win.
b4: Funds are held before any work starts. PayPal requires the buyer to approve the order, so Pact stops here and hands me the approval link instead of pretending the order is already a hold. I approve it in the real PayPal Sandbox — and this is Sandbox, so no real money moves. Back in Pact, I continue, and it authorizes the hold.
b5: The delivery is checked against every acceptance criterion by an independent verifier, and only a passing verdict releases the money. The capture is confirmed by PayPal, and every step — order, approval, hold, verification, release — is in a hash-chained ledger that can be re-verified.
b6: If I need to reverse it, the refund runs through PayPal too — capped at the captured amount and deduplicated, so asking twice never moves money twice. A failed verification would have voided the hold instead, and the buyer would be charged nothing.
b7: Pact doesn't ask strangers to trust each other blindly. It gives their agreement a payment lifecycle they can verify — a real hold, a real capture, a real refund, and a record of all three.
